analysis.one_liner: Caps federal student loan interest rates at 3% for new and consolidated federal student loans.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced with one Democratic sponsor and two Republican cosponsors in August 2024 and died in committee without a hearing, a vote, or action from either chamber.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change federal law so that new federal student loans — subsidized Stafford, unsubsidized Stafford, and PLUS loans, which are loans parents and grad students can take out up to the full cost of school — could not charge more than 3% interest. It would also let borrowers consolidate existing loans into a new federal loan capped at 3%, even if their original loans carried higher rates. Today, rates on these loans are set each spring based on a government bond formula and have run far higher in recent years.
analysis.who_benefits: Student borrowers who take out new federal loans, and borrowers who consolidate existing federal loans at the 3% rate. Millions of households pay federal student loan interest for decades, so a 3% cap would meaningfully shrink what they repay over the life of a loan. Parents borrowing PLUS loans, which currently carry among the highest federal rates, would see the biggest relief.

how_it_helps.text: New Federal Direct Stafford, Unsubsidized Stafford, and PLUS loans first disbursed on or after July 1, 2024 could not carry an interest rate above 3%.

Federal Direct Consolidation Loans issued on or after July 1, 2024 would bear interest of no more than 3%, regardless of the rates on the original loans being combined — letting existing borrowers refinance old high-rate debt.
The cap would be written directly into the Higher Education Act, so it would not float with market interest rates as current law does.

analysis.who_pays: The federal government, and ultimately taxpayers, who would collect far less interest on federal student loans. Because the government funds the loan program from the spread it earns, a 3% cap — including on high-rate PLUS loans — would sharply cut that revenue, and the bill contains no offsetting funding or spending cuts.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers and the loan program

drawbacks.text: The bill sets a rate below what the government itself pays to borrow, and it includes no funding source or offset, so the lost interest revenue to the federal student loan program would be very large.
Cheaper money for students can push tuition upward over time, a cost schools rather than borrowers would capture; the bill does nothing about what colleges charge.

The benefit only reaches people with federal loans — the roughly 3% cap does not touch private student loans, and the bill offers nothing to borrowers in default or those already repaying without consolidating.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For borrowers, the benefit is real and large: a 3% rate on a loan held for 20 years saves thousands of dollars versus rates that have recently been several times higher. The honest objection is design, not intent — the bill slashes the government's loan revenue with no offset, making its fiscal cost enormous, and cheaper credit may feed tuition inflation. Still, a straightforward interest cap for borrowers is more direct than most student debt proposals.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced at the end of August 2024 and referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee, which never held a hearing or vote, and the bill expired when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Jared Moskowitz introduced the Student Loan Interest Cap Act in the House on August 30, 2024, with Rep. Anna Paulina Luna as a cosponsor.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce the same day; no further action was ever taken on it.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so the bill died in committee without a hearing, a markup, or a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No borrower saw relief, and no industry had to absorb a cost. The federal loan program kept charging the higher rates it would have lost under the cap, and lawmakers spent no political capital on it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one; the bill simply expired

for.name: Rep. Jared Moskowitz
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill capping federal student loan interest at 3% and referred it to committee.

for.name: 2 of 224 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill alongside the Democratic sponsor.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.role: Committee of referral; sets the House agenda for education bills
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Support was small and bipartisan in form — one Democratic sponsor and two Republican cosponsors — but with three total backers the bill never generated a partisan fight; it simply received no committee action.

industries.industry: Federal student loan program (and taxpayers who fund it)
industries.note: The program's revenue comes from the interest borrowers pay, and the bill would cap that at 3%, including on high-rate PLUS and consolidation loans. The cost would fall on the federal Treasury and ultimately taxpayers.

industries.industry: Private student lenders and loan servicers
industries.note: A 3% federal consolidation option would compete with higher-rate private refinancing lenders. Servicers' contracts and collections would be largely untouched by the bill.
